title-group.article-title: The Labrador Sea as a conduit for AMOC lower-limb transport anomalies on multiple timescales

abstract.p: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is an essential element of the global climate system, yet its variability on timescales longer than those observed remains unsettled. Recent studies show that transport variability in the lower AMOC limb is maximized on density surfaces well below the density of maximum overturning. To explore the source and impact of this feature, we analyze lower-limb transport variability using climate simulations and observations from the Overturning in the Subpolar North Atlantic Program. We find that enhanced variability at select densities reflects transport redistribution within the lower limb and is not strongly linked with local or downstream AMOC variability on monthly to multidecadal timescales. Furthermore, the strong transport variability in dense waters leaving the Labrador Sea is tightly linked to variability entering the basin, with the opposing inflow and outflow largely canceling in basin-integrated diagnostics. These results underscore the need to account for density-space compensation and cancellation of opposing flows when interpreting the climatic relevance of strong subpolar transport variability.

The study shows that, despite the Labrador Sea forming the final leg of the Atlantic overturning circulation’s subpolar ‘relay’, transport changes originating in the Irminger and Iceland basins exert the strongest downstream influence.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) plays a central role in the Earth’s climate system by redistributing vast amounts of heat, salt, and carbon globally. Its upper limb carries warm waters northward from the tropics to polar latitudes, releasing heat to the atmosphere along the way, thereby impacting the weather and climate of surrounding regions1,2. As these waters lose heat, they become denser and sink, forming North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW), which includes upper NADW formed in the subpolar North Atlantic and lower NADW comprised mainly of denser overflow waters originating from the Nordic Seas. These waters constitute the AMOC lower limb that flows equatorward throughout the Atlantic.

With AMOC changes historically linked to deep water formation on various timescales2,3, oceanographers have long been interested in the amount of deep water formed in the Labrador, Irminger and Nordic Seas4–8 to understand how variability in each region impacts the AMOC. Over the past two decades, modelling studies have indicated strong links between Labrador Sea deep convection, density and AMOC variability7–10. However, summer hydrographic surveys from the 1990s11 suggested that the Labrador Sea contributes minimally to NADW volume. Consistent with these earlier estimates, direct observations from the Overturning in the Subpolar North Atlantic Program (OSNAP)12 later revealed that overturning across the eastern OSNAP section (i.e., in the Iceland and Irminger basins) dominates both the mean and monthly variability of subpolar overturning, with minimal contribution from the Labrador Sea13.

One modelling study14 attempted to reconcile the discrepancy between OSNAP observations and earlier modelling studies linking AMOC variability to Labrador Sea processes. It suggested that subsurface density anomalies in the Labrador Sea are strongly influenced by signals originating in the Irminger Sea, implying that the Labrador Sea is unlikely to be the primary source of AMOC variability. Another eddy-resolving modelling study15 showed that low-frequency AMOC anomalies at 45°N are preceded by pronounced lower-limb transport anomalies associated with enhanced water mass transformation (WMT) within the Labrador Sea Water (LSW) density range. On this basis, the authors argued that although the Labrador Sea contributes only weakly to the mean and monthly variability of the AMOC, it may play a disproportionately important role in driving low-frequency variability. Recent observational analyses, however, complicate this interpretation. While surface-forced water mass transformation accounts for a substantial fraction of the mean lower-limb transport, its variability explains only part of the AMOC variability on seasonal to interannual timescales, with the remainder arising from basin storage, interior mixing and advective processes16. Together, these studies leave unresolved how transport variability within specific density classes, including the LSW density range, relates to AMOC variability across timescales, and which density-space transport anomalies more effectively capture AMOC variability, both at the OSNAP section and farther downstream.

Here, we show that pronounced lower-limb transport variability largely reflects redistribution among density classes and, on monthly to multidecadal timescales, is only weakly related to AMOC variability at OSNAP and farther downstream. In the Labrador Sea, both the dense-water inflow and outflow correlate with AMOC variability, yet their opposing contributions largely cancel upon basin integration, thus substantially weakening the basin-scale relationship with the AMOC.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Focusing on internal variability, we analyze the first 300 years of each piControl simulation to ensure consistency across models with different run lengths. Unless otherwise indicated, all statistics reported in this study represent multimodel means. Results from two models CESM218 and MPI-ESM1-2-HR19 are used as representative examples in selected figures. OSNAP observations20 are used to assess whether the structural feature of overturning variability identified in the models are also evident in observations on monthly timescales. While direct model-observation comparisons are limited by differences in external forcings and record length, the observations provide important context for interpreting simulated variability.

sec.title: Density structure of transport variability across timescales

sec.p: Given the similar density-space structure of HF and LF variability, we focus here and in the following sections on LF variability and use multimodel results to examine how transport variability at different densities relates to the overall MOC variability. Corresponding HF results are summarized below and shown in the Supplementary Information.

sec.title: Linkage between outgoing and incoming transports in the Labrador Sea
sec.p: High-frequency variability shows the same overall behavior, with a similar density-space structure but larger amplitudes (Supplementary Fig. 10), suggesting that the key pathway signature identified here is not restricted to low-frequency variability. Together, these results indicate that transport anomalies entering the Labrador Sea are advected into the outgoing flow and modified during transit, including a modest shift toward denser densities and an amplification of variability.

sec.title: Impact on downstream MOC variability
sec.p: While our discussion focuses on the downstream MOC at 50°N, these relationships persist over a broader latitudinal range. Correlations between transport variability at the OSNAP sections and the downstream MOC remain consistent from 45°N to 60°N, with correlation strength slightly weakening and associated lead times generally increasing toward lower latitudes (Supplementary Figs. 11a, d).

Decomposition of the western basin overturning into inflow (OW-In) and outflow (OW-Out) components reveals a clearer relationship with the downstream MOC than that inferred from the basin-integrated O-West signal (Fig. 4b). Peak correlations increase to ~0.61 for OW-In and ~0.62 for OW-Out, compared with only ~0.33 for basin-integrated O-West. These directional components also correlate more clearly with the local OSNAP MOC (Supplementary Fig. 7b) and tend to lead the downstream MOC by several years (Supplementary Fig. 11), indicating that basin integration in the Labrador Sea obscures variability that is important for downstream overturning variability.

By contrast, no similar enhancement is found for O-East. The transport exiting O-East (OE-Out) shows a similarly strong relationship with the downstream MOC ( ~ 0.62), but this provides little additional correlation with the downstream MOC beyond the basin-integrated O-East overturning. Together, these results show that, when basin-wide section data are available, O-Full and O-East overturning provide the clearest indicators of downstream MOC variability. O-West becomes similarly informative only after its variability is decomposed into directional components, and even then, OW-In, OW-Out, and OE-Out are broadly comparable rather than showing a unique advantage for Labrador Sea outflow alone. Similar relationships are also found for high-frequency variability, although with systematically weaker correlations (Supplementary Fig. 12).

sec.title: Analysis of OSNAP Observations
sec.p: We now turn to OSNAP data to assess whether the key patterns identified in the model results are also evident in observations. Because the OSNAP record is relatively short (August 2014 to July 2022), the observational analysis is limited to monthly timescales.

Finally, time series of transport anomalies evaluated near the density of maximum variability for each component show that OE-Out, OW-Out, and OW-In exhibit coherent variability on monthly timescales (Fig. 5d). In particular, the observed correlation between OW-Out and OW-In ( | R | = 0.65; sign reversed for visualization) is comparable to that found in the model results on monthly (0.73; Supplementary Fig. 13d), HF (0.71) and LF (0.87) timescales. This supports the interpretation that variability entering the Labrador Sea is reflected in the outgoing transport, even on short timescales.

Together, the OSNAP observations support the key elements of the model-based picture. On monthly timescales, transport variability exhibits partial compensation across adjacent density classes, although this compensation is more broadly distributed in density space than in the low-frequency model results. The eastern subpolar basin contributes most to monthly OSNAP MOC variability, and transport exiting the Labrador Sea remains strongly linked to upstream variability though modified during transit through the basin. These results indicate that, although the relative importance of individual processes varies with timescale, the structural relationships among density-space variability, pathway coherence, and overturning variability are consistent between models and observations.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Across the model ensemble, variability in the eastern subpolar basin exhibits stronger correlations with both the OSNAP MOC and the downstream MOC than variability in the western basin across most density classes and timescales. This result is consistent with previous studies highlighting the dominant role of the Irminger and Iceland basins in shaping the AMOC mean state and variability13,22.

Although basin-integrated overturning in the western subpolar basin exhibits only weak correlations with the downstream MOC in the multimodel mean, decomposing the western (Labrador) basin into its northward inflow and southward outflow components reveals a markedly stronger relationship. This contrast arises because inflow and outflow anomalies are strongly correlated yet opposite in sign, so their lateral integration across the basin leads to partial cancellation, contributing to the weak relationship between basin-integrated western overturning and overall MOC variability. At the same time, the broadly similar correlations of OE-Out, OW-In, and OW-Out with the downstream AMOC indicate that variability most relevant to downstream overturning is already present in the transport exiting OSNAP East. As shown in previous studies, the signal exiting OE-Out mainly reflects buoyancy-forced transformation in the Iceland and Irminger basins, as well as the broader eastern subpolar basin23,24. This variability is subsequently advected into the Labrador Sea, where it is modified, often amplified and shifted toward denser classes during transit25. Despite these modifications, its relationship with the downstream AMOC is largely unchanged from that exiting OSNAP-East. This interpretation is supported by the comparison between OW-In and Labrador Sea SFWMT: OW-In explains substantially more variance in OW-Out than SFWMT, and including both increases explained variance only modestly. Consistent with recent work suggesting that dense waters exported from the Labrador Sea reflect cumulative transformation across the broader subpolar gyre, rather than formation within a single localized region26–28, these results indicate that the Labrador Sea acts primarily as a conduit for transport anomalies linked to AMOC strength variability. This conduit interpretation refers specifically to the incoming and exported Labrador Sea transport anomalies, which are connected to transport variability exiting OSNAP-East and are significantly correlated with downstream and OSNAP-Full MOC strength. It does not imply that the local Labrador Sea overturning residual is inherited directly from upstream. OSNAP observations, despite their limited duration and restriction to monthly timescales, support this interpretation by revealing similar compensating structures and strong correlations between incoming and outgoing transports across OSNAP-West.

This framework helps reconcile our results with previous studies emphasizing the importance of Labrador Sea water mass transformation for downstream AMOC variability15. Our results do not argue against such a contribution. Rather, they suggest that across the broader model ensemble, Labrador Sea SFWMT explains only part of the downstream signal. That downstream signal, expressed as AMOC variability at 50°N, is more consistently reflected in the upstream transport anomalies (OE-Out, OW-In, and OW-Out) than in SFWMT. Thus, although Labrador Sea transformation can modify the dense signal, it does not emerge as the dominant or most robust control on downstream AMOC variability across models. This distinction is important for identifying indicators of the downstream MOC. When basin-wide section data are available, O-East and O-Full provide the clearest measures of downstream AMOC strength, whereas decomposing Labrador Sea overturning into inflow and outflow components helps recover the downstream-relevant variability that is obscured in the basin-integrated western overturning in the Labrador Sea.

These conclusions should be interpreted with awareness of the limitation of CMIP6 climate models in the subpolar North Atlantic. Models differ substantially in stratification, overflow representation, and the location and intensity of deep convection and water mass transformation, particularly in the Labrador Sea, leading to large inter-model spread in density structure and variability26,28–30. Our aim is therefore not to quantify absolute overturning or water mass transformation in any individual region, nor to attribute all model differences to a single mechanism. Instead, it focuses on the structural relationship between transport variability across density classes and integrated overturning that persist across models and are also evident in observations. Across the CMIP6 ensemble, key features, such as strong variability in dense waters, compensation across density classes, coherent pathway evolution, and the weak projection of dense variability onto overturning strength, emerge despite model spread. Similar structural signatures are also evident in OSNAP observations on monthly timescales, lending observational support to the mechanisms identified here. In that sense, the value of the multimodel framework here is not to provide a single deterministic picture, but to identify which features emerge robustly despite large differences in model mean state and variability.

sec.title: Calculation of the MOC
Temporal filtering
sec.p: For all model simulations, monthly output from the first 300 years of the preindustrial control (piControl) integrations is used. Annual means are computed from the monthly data prior to filtering. Low-frequency (LF) variability is isolated using a fourth-order Butterworth low-pass digital filter with a 20-year cutoff period, while high-frequency (HF) variability is obtained using a Butterworth high-pass filter with a 10-year cutoff. Sensitivity tests using alternative cutoff periods (e.g. 10 and 15 years for the low-pass filter) yield qualitatively similar results and do not affect the main conclusions. For OSNAP observations, the shorter record length limits the analysis to monthly timescales. No temporal filtering is applied unless explicitly stated.

sec.title: Composite analysis and decomposition
sec.p: All composites are constructed from the filtered LF or HF time series, depending on the application described in the main text.

sec.title: Alignment across models in density space
Correlation analyses
Surface-forced water mass transformation
Observations and models
sec.p: Observational estimates of the overturning circulation are based on data from the Overturning in the Subpolar North Atlantic Program (OSNAP). We use eight years of monthly OSNAP observations spanning August 2014 to July 2022, covering the full OSNAP section (O-Full) and its two coast-to-coast subsections, O-West and O-East (Fig. 1a). The OSNAP observing system provides gridded property and velocity fields, MOC and other time series across the section, derived from a combination of moored instruments, gliders, and ship-based measurements. The processing steps include quality control, interpolation to a common grid, and the calculation of transports in density coordinates, following established methodologies32. We use the gridded temperature, salinity, and velocity products to compute the overturning streamfunction and associated transport diagnostics in density space, consistent with previous OSNAP-based studies19.

We analyze simulations from nine coupled climate models participating in CMIP6 together with one high-resolution coupled model (CESM1.3-HR), using 300 years from each preindustrial control simulation to isolate internally generated variability. The full list of models and their key characteristics are provided in Supplementary Table 1.

The resulting ensemble spans six distinct ocean model formulations, with two model pairs differing primarily in horizontal resolution, providing a range of subpolar circulation representations without targeting specific processes. The nine CMIP6 models were drawn from the CMIP6 archive based on the availability of long preindustrial control simulations and the three-dimensional fields required for density-space diagnostics. We used Heuzé et al.29 as a broad reference to exclude models with extreme bottom-density biases in the Greenland–Iceland–Norwegian Seas and subpolar gyre, which could possibly dominate density-space structure and hinder inter-model comparison. Beyond this exclusion of clear outliers, no selection was made based on overturning behavior. Thus, the final ensemble represents a quasi-random subset spanning a range of ocean model formulations and horizontal resolutions. Accordingly, our analysis does not rely on the fidelity of any individual model, but instead emphasizes relationships that are consistent across models, timescales, and independent observations.

To ensure consistency with observational diagnostics, model output is first interpolated onto the OSNAP section grid, and velocity components are rotated to obtain the section-normal velocity. The overturning streamfunction and associated transport metrics are then computed using the same methodology as applied to OSNAP observations.

While our primary results are based on multimodel statistics, two individual models are used in selected figures for illustration. MPI-ESM1-2-HR is shown in Fig. 3a because the correlation between OW-Out and OW-In in this model is close to the multimodel mean, making it a representative example of the ensemble behavior. CESM2 is used in selected figures to illustrate the mean overturning structure and spatial patterns of variability. Neither model is chosen for superior performance; rather, the qualitative behaviors highlighted are representative of those found across the ensemble.

notes.title: Data availability
notes.p: The CMIP6 pre-industrial control (piControl) model output used in this study, including thetao, so, uo, and vo from the r1i1p1f1 ensemble member, is publicly available through the Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF; https://metagrid.esgf-west.org/search/cmip6/). The models and dataset specifications are listed in Supplementary Table 1. The CESM1.3-HR pre-industrial control simulation is publicly available through the International Laboratory for High-Resolution Earth System Prediction (iHESP; https://ihesp.github.io/archive/products/ds_archive/Datasets.html). The OSNAP gridded temperature, salinity, and velocity fields for 2014–2020 are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.35090/gatech/70342. The processed data underlying the figures are publicly available at https://github.com/jchenocean/North-Atlantic-AMOC-1Variability. Source data are provided with this paper.
